text: This is Attune. Pages that negotiate with your agent, not track you.

caption: Sixty-eight, low vision, in bed at night: “Does a 1% fee matter over 40 years?” Her agent already knows all that.
text: Sixty-eight years old, low vision, reading in bed at night: does a one percent fee matter over forty years? Her agent already knows all of that. Watch what happens when it tells the page.

caption: Two tool calls. A 3-minute edition from the author’s blocks, on a screen designed for her — with reasons.
text: Two tool calls. The page composed a three-minute edition from the author's own blocks, skipping what she already knows. Nothing generated. And it chose the screen: dark, extra large, hyperlegible, big controls. Every choice has a reason in the panel, and she can change or erase any of it.

caption: The calculator is a tool too. The agent gets the same numbers she sees.
text: The calculator is a tool too. Five hundred a month, forty years, a one percent fee. The chart on the page changes, and the agent gets the exact numbers she is looking at.

caption: Two bad options today: be tracked, or be summarized. WebMCP makes a third way possible.
text: Why does this need WebMCP? Reading with an AI beside you used to mean two bad options: let the site track you, or let the AI scrape and summarize, losing the figures, the interactives, the author's voice, sometimes the facts. A header can say Korean. Only a tool call can say three minutes, knows compounding, low vision, dark room, from the agent that already knows you, with you watching.

caption: The author’s agent drafts the missing versions. The author approves by click. Readers get only what was approved.
text: And the other side of the page. In the author studio, the author's own agent reads where the article is thin and drafts the missing versions: a plainer rewrite, a beginner version, an F A Q entry. Each draft lands next to its source, pending. Approving is a click, never a tool. Readers' agents compose only from what the author approved.

caption: Three levels, two languages, all written by the author. Editions are composed, never generated.
text: Now the full beginner edition, in Korean. Every sentence in every edition was written by the author, in both languages. A deterministic composer decides trimming, order and prerequisites, and tells you why each block is in or out.

caption: The page notices where she got stuck. The agent swaps in the author’s plainer version.
text: The page notices, locally, when she re-reads a paragraph. Her agent asks where she got stuck, and swaps in the author's plainer version of that exact block, right where she is.

caption: Ask the author: answers in the author’s own words, or “not covered”. Then: forget me.
text: Questions go to the author, not to a guess: the author's own written answers, or a plain not covered. And when she says forget me, the page erases everything it knew.

caption: For publishers: anonymous demand signals. No identifiers, ever.
text: For the publisher, the server only ever stores a count of which editions readers asked for. What they asked for, never who they are. Any site can do this: it is a content model and a dozen small tools, not a platform.

caption: Tool surfaces follow the page. The page owns the variants; the agent owns the context; the human owns the decision.
text: Under the hood: three tool surfaces swapped with abort signals, thirty-eight tools across reader, home and studio, read-only hints on reads, a needs-to-design resolver the page owns, three original articles at three levels in two languages, sixteen unit tests, six end-to-end tests that drive every tool like an agent, and a judge mode that runs the whole negotiation with one click.
Attune. Bring your agent. The page will meet you where you are. Attune dot znehraks dot workers dot dev.
